blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Wavefronts: A wavefront is a surface of constant phase. In a homogeneous medium, the wavefront is always perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation.

Characteristics of Wavefront :

• The phase difference between various particles on the wavefront is zero.

• These wavefronts travel with the speed of light in all directions in an isotropic medium.

• A point source of light always gives rise to a spherical wavefront in an isotropic medium.

• Normal to the wavefront represents a ray of light.

• It always travels in the forward direction in the medium.

Law of reflection by Huygen's wave Theory: $\sin i=\sin r$

Law of refraction by Huygen's wave Theory: $\mu_1 \sin i=\mu_2 \sin r$

(1) Coherent sources : Two light sources are said to be coherent if they emit light waves of the same frequency and have a constant phase difference. They are obtained from a single source.

(2) Incoherent sources : Two sources are said to be incoherent if their phase difference changes with time. Two independent monochromatic sources of same frequency are incoherent because atoms cannot emit light waves in same phase and thesesources are said to be incoherent sources.

Methods of Obtaining Coherent Source :

(1) Division of wavefront: In this method, the wavefront is divided into two or more parts by reflection or refraction using mirrors, lenses, prisms, or slits.

(2) Division of Amplitude : The amplitude of the incoming beam is divided in two parts either by parallel reflection or refraction. These divided parts reunite after traversing different paths and produce interference.

Huygen's Principal:

• Each point on a wavefront is a source of new disturbance, called secondary wavelets. These Wavelets are spherical and travel with the speed of light in that medium.

• The forward envelope of the secondary wavelets at any instant gives the new wavefront.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
Which of the following does NOT directly follow from Huygen's Principle?

A) Diffraction of light

B) Refraction of light

C) The formation of shadows

D) The straight-line propagation of light in uniform media
blocks.answer:
Correct Answer: D) The straight-line propagation of light in uniform media

While Huygen’s Principle helps explain diffraction and refraction, it is not necessary for the straight-line propagation of light in uniform media, which is explained by basic ray optics. In a uniform medium, light naturally travels in straight lines without any deviation, which is a direct consequence of the principles of ray optics rather than Huygen’s Principle.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Misunderstanding Secondary Wavelet Direction: Assuming wavelets propagate randomly instead of spherically from each point on the wavefront.
  • Incorrect Wavefront Prediction: Expecting planar wavefronts after diffraction rather than spherical.
  • Confusing Rays and Wavefronts: Forgetting rays are perpendicular to wavefronts and indicate energy propagation.
  • Ignoring Medium Changes: Not considering how wavefronts and speed change when passing through different media.

modules.name: Interference of Light And Young's Double Slit Experiment

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Interference of Light:- When the waves emitting from the coherent sources propagating in the same direction are superposed over one another, then redistribution of energy takes place in space and this phenomenon is called interference. It obeys the law of conservation of energy.

• Resultant amplitude:  $A_{\text {res }}=\sqrt{A_1^2+A_2^2+2 A_1 A_2 \cos \Delta \phi}$

• Phase angle:  $\theta=\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\mathrm{~A}_2 \sin \phi}{\mathrm{~A}_1+\mathrm{A}_2 \cos \phi}\right)$

• Resultant intensity:  $\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{I}_1+\mathrm{I}_2+2 \sqrt{\mathrm{I}_1} \sqrt{\mathrm{I}_2} \cos \Delta \phi$

$2 \sqrt{I_1} \sqrt{I_2} \cos \Delta \phi $  is known as interference factor.

Average intensity of interference pattern $=\frac{\mathrm{I}_{\max }+\mathrm{I}_{\min }}{2}=\mathrm{I}_1+\mathrm{I}_2$

• $\text { Intensity } \propto \text { width of slit } \propto(\text { amplitude })^2 \Rightarrow I \propto W \propto A^2 \Rightarrow \frac{I_1}{I_2}=\frac{w_1}{w_2}=\frac{A_1^2}{A_2^2}$
      • $\frac{I_{\max }}{I_{\min }}=\left[\frac{\sqrt{I_1}+\sqrt{I_2}}{\sqrt{I_1}-\sqrt{I_2}}\right]^2=\left[\frac{A_1+A_2}{A_1-A_2}\right]^2=\left[\frac{A_{\max }}{A_{\min }}\right]^2$

• $\text { Fringe visibility } V=\frac{I_{\max }-I_{\min }}{I_{\max }+I_{\min }} \times 100 \% \text { when } I_{\min }=0 \text { then fringe visibility is maximum. }$
Conditions for sustained interference :

• The two sources should be coherent.

• The separation between two coherent sources should be small.

• The distance of the screen from the two sources should be large.

• For good contrast between maxima and minima, the amplitude of two interfering waves should be as nearly equal as possible.

Young’s Double Slit Experiment (Y.D.S.E.) : According to Huygens, light is a wave. It is proved experimentally by YDSE. In YDSE division of wavefront takes place.

• At point O path difference and phase difference of the waves coming from the source via both the slit is zero.
        • The fringe formed at the point O is known as central maxima or central bright fringe.
If bright fringe is formed at point P :

$\Delta \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{n} \lambda$

$\frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{D}}=\mathrm{n} \lambda$

$\mathrm{y}=\frac{\mathrm{n} \lambda \mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{~d}}$

Distance of $ \mathrm{n}^{\text {th }} $maxima from central maxima

$\mathrm{y}_{\text {max }_{\mathrm{m}^{\mathrm{th}}}}=\frac{\mathrm{n} \lambda \mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{~d}}$

If dark fringe is formed at point P :

$\Delta \mathrm{x}=\frac{(2 \mathrm{n}-1) \lambda}{2}$

$\frac{d y}{D}=\frac{(2 n-1) \lambda}{2}$

$\mathrm{y}=\frac{(2 \mathrm{n}-1) \lambda \mathrm{D}}{2 \mathrm{~d}}$

Distance of $ n^{\text {th }} $minima from central maxima

$\mathrm{y}_{\min _{\mathrm{nth}}}=\frac{(2 \mathrm{n}-1) \lambda \mathrm{D}}{2 \mathrm{~d}}$

blocks.title: Keypoints
blocks.text:
• Fringes are neither image nor shadow of a slit but the locus of a point which moves in such a way that its path difference from the two sources remains constant.

• In YDSE the interference fringes for two coherent point sources are hyperboloids with axis $\mathrm{S}_1 \mathrm{~S}_2 .$

• No interference pattern is detected when two coherent sources are infinitely close to each other, because $\beta \propto \frac{1}{d}$.

modules.name: Fringe Width And Thin Film Interference

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Fringe width :Distance between two successive dark fringes or two successive bright fringes is known as fringe width.

$\beta=\frac{\lambda D}{d}$

Dark fringe width:

$\beta=\frac{2 \lambda D}{d}-\frac{1 \lambda D}{d} \Rightarrow \beta=\frac{\lambda D}{d}$

Bright fringe width:

$\beta=\frac{3 \lambda D}{2 d}-\frac{\lambda D}{2 d} \Rightarrow \quad \boldsymbol{\beta}=\frac{\lambda D}{d}$

Angular fringe width : It is the angle subtended by linear fringe width at the centre of the plane of slit.

$\begin{aligned} & \alpha=\frac{\beta}{D} \\ & \alpha=\frac{\lambda D}{d D} \\ & \alpha=\frac{\lambda}{d} \end{aligned}$

Angular fringe width does not depend on the distance between plane of slit and screen.

Variation of intensity with phase difference:

If slits are of equal width then intensity is also equal.

$\mathrm{I}=4 \mathrm{I}_0 \cos ^2\left(\frac{\Delta \phi}{2}\right)$

Effect of white light in YDSE:

  • The interference patterns due to different component colours of white light overlap (incoherently). The central bright fringes for different colour are at the same position. Therefore, the central fringe is white.
  • The  fringe closest on either side of the central white fringe is red and the farthest will appear blue. After a few fringes, no clear fringe pattern is seen.
Thin Film in Front of a Slit in YDSE:  If a transparent sheet of refractive index μ and thickness t is introduced in one of the paths of interfering waves, the optical path will become 'μt' instead of 't'.

Entire fringe pattern is displaced towards the side in Which the thin sheet is introduced without any change in fringe width.

$\text { Path difference produced by a slab } \Delta x=(\mu-1) \mathrm{t}$

• $\text { Fringe shift, } y=\frac{D}{d}(\mu-1) t$

• $\text { Number of fringes shift }=\frac{\text { shift }}{\text { fringe width }}=\frac{\mathrm{t}(\mu-1) \mathrm{D} / \mathrm{d}}{\lambda \mathrm{D} / \mathrm{d}}=\frac{(\mu-1) \mathrm{t}}{\lambda}$

Note : When thin film is placed in front of both the slit then central maxima is shifted to that side where the path difference due to slab is more.

      • $\text { Fringe shift }=\frac{\left(\left(\mu_2-1\right) \mathrm{t}_2-\left(\mu_1-1\right) \mathrm{t}_1\right) \mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{~d}}$

• $\text { Number of fringes shift }=\frac{\left(\left(\mu_2-1\right) t_2-\left(\mu_1-1\right) t_1\right)}{\lambda}$

Path difference in Thin Film Interference:

1. Reflected System

Maxima- $2 \mu \mathrm{t} \cos \mathrm{r}-\frac{\lambda}{2}=\mathrm{n} \lambda$    Minima- $2 \mu t \cos r-\frac{\lambda}{2}=\frac{(2 n-1) \lambda}{2}$

2.Transmitted System

Maxima- $2 \mu \mathrm{t} \cos \mathrm{r}=\mathrm{n} \lambda$      Minima- $2 \mu t \cos r=\frac{(2 n-1) \lambda}{2}$

For thin film interference to be observable, thickness of film must be in order of wavelength of light $\left(\approx 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}\right)$

Note: For the reflected system if thickness of the thin film tends to zero then thin film appears dark.

$\Delta \mathrm{x}=2 \mu \mathrm{t} \operatorname{cosr}-\frac{\lambda}{2}$

$|\Delta x|=\frac{\lambda}{2} \quad(\text { When, } t \approx 0)$

This condition represents destructive interference therefore dark fringes are formed.

Note:

    • Whenever a wave is reflected from a denser medium, an extra phase difference of π or path difference of λ/2 is introduced.

• Whenever a wave is reflected from a rarer medium, no extra phase difference or path difference is introduced.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
Monochromatic light of wavelength $5000 \AA$ is used in YDSE, with slit width, d = 1mm, distance between screen and slits, D = 1M. If intensities at the two slits are

$I_1=4 I_0 \text { and } I_2=I_0,$ find:

a. fringe width $\beta$

b. distance of 5th minima from the central maxima on the screen,

c. intensity at $y=\frac{1}{3} m m$

d. distance of the $1000_{th}$ maxima, and

e. distance of the $5000_{th}$ maxima.
blocks.answer:
$\text { a. } \beta=\frac{\lambda D}{d}=\frac{5000 \times 10^{-10} \times 1}{1 \times 10^{-3}}=0.5 \mathrm{~mm}$

$\text { b. } y=(2 n-1) \frac{\lambda D}{\alpha}, n=5 \Rightarrow y=2.25 m m$

$\text { c. At } y=\dfrac{1}{3} m m, y<<D \Rightarrow \Delta x=\dfrac{d y}{D}$

$\Delta\phi=\dfrac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \times \dfrac{d y}{D}$$=\Delta \phi=\dfrac{2 \pi d y}{\lambda D}$

$\begin{aligned} &\Delta\phi =\frac{2 \pi \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m} \times  \frac{1}{3} \times 10^{-2}}{5000 \times 10^{-10} \times {1}} \\ & \Delta\phi=\frac{4 \pi}{3} \end{aligned}$

Now, Resultant Intensity,

$I=I_1+I_2+2 \cos (\Delta \phi)=4 I_0+I_0+2 \sqrt{4 I_0^2} \cos (\Delta \phi)$

$5 I_0+4 I_0 \cos \left(\frac{4 \pi}{3}\right)=3 I_0$

$\text { d. } \frac{d}{\lambda}=\frac{10^3}{0.5 \times 10^6}=2000$

Hence, now $\Delta x=d \sin \theta$ must be used.

$\therefore d \sin \theta=n \lambda=1000 \lambda \Rightarrow \sin \theta=1000 \frac{\lambda}{d}=\frac{1}{2}$

$\Rightarrow \theta=30^{\circ}$

$y=D \tan \theta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} m$

e. Highest Order Maxima, $n_{\max }=\left[\frac{d}{\lambda}\right]=2000$

Hence, n = 5000 is not possible.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Diffraction:

Bending of light rays from sharp edges of an opaque obstacle or aperture and its spreading in the geometrical shadow region is defined as diffraction of light or deviation of light from its rectilinear propagation tendency is defined as diffraction of light.

Conditions of Diffraction:

Path difference at any point on screen due to Fraunhofer diffraction:

$\text { Path difference, } \Delta x=a \sin \theta$

• Size of obstacle or aperture should be nearly equal (Comparable) to the wavelength.

• If size of obstacle/aperture is much larger than wavelength, then diffraction is not observable. (It is practically observed when size of aperture or obstacle is greater than 50λ. The obstacle or aperture does not show diffraction.)

Types of Diffraction

Fresnel diffraction: Both source and screen are near the diffraction device.

Fraunhofer diffraction: Both source and screen are effectively at infinite distances from the diffracting device.

Single slit Diffraction:

$\text {For } n^{\text {th }} \text { secondary minima; } \operatorname{a\sin \theta=n} \lambda \Rightarrow y=\frac{n \lambda D}{a}$

$\text {For } n^{\text {th }} \text { secondary maxima; } a\sin \theta=\frac{(2 n+1) \lambda}{2} \Rightarrow y=\frac{(2 n+1) \lambda D}{2 a}$

$\text{For Central Bright Fringe, Linear width of} \mathrm{CBF}=\frac{2 \lambda \mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{a}}; Angular width of \mathrm{CBF}=2 \sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\mathrm{a}}\right)$

Intensity in Diffraction:

$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{I} & =\mathrm{I}_0\left[\frac{\sin (\beta / 2)}{\beta / 2}\right]^2 \text { and } \beta=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \mathrm{a} \sin \theta \\ I_0 & =\text { intensity of central maxima } \end{aligned}$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
1. Misunderstanding the Diffraction Condition: Confusing the conditions for maxima and minima. For single-slit diffraction, maxima occur when $a \sin \theta=\left(m+\frac{1}{2}\right) \lambda$ , and minima occur when $a \sin \theta=m \lambda$ (for minima).

2. Misapplying Conditions for Multiple Slits: Confusing maxima and minima conditions.

3. Wrong Angle Range: Calculating angles beyond  $90^{\circ}$.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Polarisation of Light Wave: The phenomenon of restricting the vibration of light (electric vector) in a particular direction perpendicular to the direction of propagation of wave is called polarisation of light.

• Polarisation confirms the transverse nature of wave.

• Longitudinal waves (Ultrasonic wave, sonic wave, infrasonic wave etc.) cannot be polarised.

Unpolarised light:  A beam of unpolarised light consists of waves moving in the same direction with their electric vectors pointed in random orientations about the axis of propagation.

Polarised light: If the vibrations of a wave are present in just one direction in a plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation, the wave is said to be polarised or plane polarised.

Polariser: Polariser is any device or crystal that can convert an unpolarised light into Polarised light. e.g. : Tourmaline crystal , Nicol Prism etc.

Analyser: Analyser is a device which is used to determine whether the light is Plane polarised or not. Analyser and Polariser are made up of same material only placement position is different.

Optic axis/Transmission axis: The axis along which light gets polarised after passing through a polariser.

Plane Polarised Light

Plane of Vibration: Plane in which Electric and Magnetic field vibrates/oscillates is known as plane of vibration.

Plane of Polarisation: Plane which is perpendicular to plane of vibration.

Polarisation of light: If the vibrations of a wave are present in just one direction in a plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation, the wave is said to be polarised or plane polarised.

Polarisation by Dichroism/Selective absorption:

• Some crystals such as tourmaline and sheets of iodosulphate of quinone have the property of strongly absorbing the light with vibrations perpendicular of a specific direction (called transmission axis) and transmitting the light with vibration parallel to it. This selective absorption of light is called dichroism.
    • So, if unpolarised light passes through proper thickness of these crystals, the transmitted light will plane polarised with vibrations parallel to transmission axis.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Malus' Law : When Plane Polarised Light (PPL) of intensity $I_0$ passes through a polaroid such that angle between Axis of vibration of PPL and Optic Axis of Polaroid is θ, then Intensity of Emergent Light after passing through Polaroid becomes ,

$I=I_0 \cos ^2 \theta$

When analyser is rotated by 360° in front of polariser :

Observations :

• After passing through polariser, intensity of light becomes half.
    • Final intensity is maximum two times.
    • Final intensity becomes zero two times.

Polarisation by Reflection : When unpolarised light is incident on the interface of two medium such that reflected and refracted ray are mutually perpendicular to each other than reflected ray is perfectly polarised normal to plane of incidence and refracted ray in the same plane is partially polarised.

$\begin{aligned} &\text{By Snell's Law, } \mu_1 \sin \theta_P = \mu_2 \sin r \\ &\mu_1 \sin \theta_{\text{P}} = \mu_2 \sin \left(90^\circ - \theta_{\text{P}}\right) \\ &\mu_1 \sin \theta_{\text{P}} = \mu_2 \cos \left(\theta_{\text{P}}\right) \\ &\frac{\sin \theta_{\text{P}}}{\cos \theta_{\text{P}}} = \frac{\mu_2}{\mu_1} \\ &\tan \theta_{\text{P}} = \frac{\mu_2}{\mu_1}  \end{aligned}$

(where  $\theta_{\text{P}}$ is the polarizing angle, or Brewster's angle).

Brewster's Law: The tangent of polarising angle of incidence at which reflected light becomes completely plane polarised is numerically equal to refractive index of the medium.

$\mu=\operatorname{tan}i_p$

$i_p=\text { Brewster's angle and } i_p+r_p=90^{\circ}$

Polarisation by Refraction: When a light wave travels from one medium to another, it changes its direction and speed. This refracted beam attains some degree of polarization; therefore, after passing through a number of media, emerging light will become plane polarised with vibrations in the plane of paper.

Polarisation by Scattering:- When light scatters on small particles such as dust, air molecules, it gets absorbed by electrons in the atoms and re-radiated in all directions.

• Light scattered in a plane at right angle to the incident light is always plane polarised.

Polarisation by Double Refraction:-It was found that in certain crystals such as calcite, quartz and tourmaline, etc., incident unpolarised light splits into two light beams of equal intensities with perpendicular polarisations.

• One of the rays behaves as ordinary light (obeys law of refraction) is called O-ray (ordinary ray) while the other which does not obey laws of refraction is called E-ray (extra-ordinary ray).
    • When an object is seen through these crystals is rotated, one image (due to E-ray) rotates around the other (due to O-ray).

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
A plane polarized beam of intensity I is incident on a polarizer with the electric vector inclined at 30o to the optic axis of the polarizer. Light coming out of the polarizer through an analyser whose optic axis is inclined at 30o to the polarizer. Find the intensity of light coming out of the analyser.

(A) $\frac{I}{4}$

(B) $\frac{9I}{16}$

(C) $\frac{I}{16}$

(D) $\frac{16 I}{9}$
blocks.answer:
Ans. (B)

Using Malus' Law:

$I_1=I \cos ^2\left(30^{\circ}\right)$

$I_1=\frac{3}{4} I$

Using Malus' Law Again:

$I_2=I_1 \cos ^2\left(\theta_2\right)$

$I_2=I_1 \cos ^2\left(30^{\circ}\right)$

$\text { Substituting } I_1 \text { : }$

$\begin{aligned} & I_2=\frac{3}{4} I \cdot \cos ^2\left(30^{\circ}\right) \\ & I_2=\frac{3}{4} I \cdot\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2 \\ & I_2=\frac{3}{4} I \cdot \frac{3}{4} \\ & I_2=\frac{9}{16} I \end{aligned}$

• Resultant amplitude:  $A_{\text {res }}=\sqrt{A_1^2+A_2^2+2 A_1 A_2 \cos \Delta \phi}$

• Phase angle:  $\theta=\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\mathrm{~A}_2 \sin \phi}{\mathrm{~A}_1+\mathrm{A}_2 \cos \phi}\right)$

• Resultant intensity:  $\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{I}_1+\mathrm{I}_2+2 \sqrt{\mathrm{I}_1} \sqrt{\mathrm{I}_2} \cos \Delta \phi$

$2 \sqrt{I_1} \sqrt{I_2} \cos \Delta \phi $  is known as interference factor.

Average intensity of interference pattern $=\frac{\mathrm{I}_{\max }+\mathrm{I}_{\min }}{2}=\mathrm{I}_1+\mathrm{I}_2$

• $\text { Intensity } \propto \text { width of slit } \propto(\text { amplitude })^2 \Rightarrow I \propto W \propto A^2 \Rightarrow \frac{I_1}{I_2}=\frac{w_1}{w_2}=\frac{A_1^2}{A_2^2}$
      • $\frac{I_{\max }}{I_{\min }}=\left[\frac{\sqrt{I_1}+\sqrt{I_2}}{\sqrt{I_1}-\sqrt{I_2}}\right]^2=\left[\frac{A_1+A_2}{A_1-A_2}\right]^2=\left[\frac{A_{\max }}{A_{\min }}\right]^2$

• $\text { Fringe visibility } V=\frac{I_{\max }-I_{\min }}{I_{\max }+I_{\min }} \times 100 \% \text { when } I_{\min }=0 \text { then fringe visibility is maximum. }$
Conditions for sustained interference :

• The two sources should be coherent.

• The separation between two coherent sources should be small.

• The distance of the screen from the two sources should be large.

• For good contrast between maxima and minima, the amplitude of two interfering waves should be as nearly equal as possible.

Young’s Double Slit Experiment (Y.D.S.E.) : According to Huygens, light is a wave. It is proved experimentally by YDSE. In YDSE division of wavefront takes place.

• At point O path difference and phase difference of the waves coming from the source via both the slit is zero.
        • The fringe formed at the point O is known as central maxima or central bright fringe.
If bright fringe is formed at point P :

$\Delta \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{n} \lambda$

$\frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{D}}=\mathrm{n} \lambda$

$\mathrm{y}=\frac{\mathrm{n} \lambda \mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{~d}}$

Distance of $ \mathrm{n}^{\text {th }} $maxima from central maxima

$\mathrm{y}_{\text {max }_{\mathrm{m}^{\mathrm{th}}}}=\frac{\mathrm{n} \lambda \mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{~d}}$

If dark fringe is formed at point P :

$\Delta \mathrm{x}=\frac{(2 \mathrm{n}-1) \lambda}{2}$

$\frac{d y}{D}=\frac{(2 n-1) \lambda}{2}$

$\mathrm{y}=\frac{(2 \mathrm{n}-1) \lambda \mathrm{D}}{2 \mathrm{~d}}$

Distance of $ n^{\text {th }} $minima from central maxima

$\mathrm{y}_{\min _{\mathrm{nth}}}=\frac{(2 \mathrm{n}-1) \lambda \mathrm{D}}{2 \mathrm{~d}}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Fringe width :Distance between two successive dark fringes or two successive bright fringes is known as fringe width.

$\beta=\frac{\lambda D}{d}$

Dark fringe width:

$\beta=\frac{2 \lambda D}{d}-\frac{1 \lambda D}{d} \Rightarrow \beta=\frac{\lambda D}{d}$

Bright fringe width:

$\beta=\frac{3 \lambda D}{2 d}-\frac{\lambda D}{2 d} \Rightarrow \quad \boldsymbol{\beta}=\frac{\lambda D}{d}$

Angular fringe width : It is the angle subtended by linear fringe width at the centre of the plane of slit.

$\begin{aligned} & \alpha=\frac{\beta}{D} \\ & \alpha=\frac{\lambda D}{d D} \\ & \alpha=\frac{\lambda}{d} \end{aligned}$

Angular fringe width does not depend on the distance between plane of slit and screen.

Variation of intensity with phase difference:

If slits are of equal width then intensity is also equal.

$\mathrm{I}=4 \mathrm{I}_0 \cos ^2\left(\frac{\Delta \phi}{2}\right)$

Effect of white light in YDSE:

  • The interference patterns due to different component colours of white light overlap (incoherently). The central bright fringes for different colour are at the same position. Therefore, the central fringe is white.
  • The  fringe closest on either side of the central white fringe is red and the farthest will appear blue. After a few fringes, no clear fringe pattern is seen.
Thin Film in Front of a Slit in YDSE:  If a transparent sheet of refractive index μ and thickness t is introduced in one of the paths of interfering waves, the optical path will become 'μt' instead of 't'.

Entire fringe pattern is displaced towards the side in Which the thin sheet is introduced without any change in fringe width.

$\text { Path difference produced by a slab } \Delta x=(\mu-1) \mathrm{t}$

• $\text { Fringe shift, } y=\frac{D}{d}(\mu-1) t$

• $\text { Number of fringes shift }=\frac{\text { shift }}{\text { fringe width }}=\frac{\mathrm{t}(\mu-1) \mathrm{D} / \mathrm{d}}{\lambda \mathrm{D} / \mathrm{d}}=\frac{(\mu-1) \mathrm{t}}{\lambda}$

Note : When thin film is placed in front of both the slit then central maxima is shifted to that side where the path difference due to slab is more.

      • $\text { Fringe shift }=\frac{\left(\left(\mu_2-1\right) \mathrm{t}_2-\left(\mu_1-1\right) \mathrm{t}_1\right) \mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{~d}}$

• $\text { Number of fringes shift }=\frac{\left(\left(\mu_2-1\right) t_2-\left(\mu_1-1\right) t_1\right)}{\lambda}$

Path difference in Thin Film Interference:

1. Reflected System

Maxima- $2 \mu \mathrm{t} \cos \mathrm{r}-\frac{\lambda}{2}=\mathrm{n} \lambda$    Minima- $2 \mu t \cos r-\frac{\lambda}{2}=\frac{(2 n-1) \lambda}{2}$

2.Transmitted System

Maxima- $2 \mu \mathrm{t} \cos \mathrm{r}=\mathrm{n} \lambda$      Minima- $2 \mu t \cos r=\frac{(2 n-1) \lambda}{2}$

For thin film interference to be observable, thickness of film must be in order of wavelength of light $\left(\approx 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}\right)$

Note: For the reflected system if thickness of the thin film tends to zero then thin film appears dark.

$\Delta \mathrm{x}=2 \mu \mathrm{t} \operatorname{cosr}-\frac{\lambda}{2}$

$|\Delta x|=\frac{\lambda}{2} \quad(\text { When, } t \approx 0)$

This condition represents destructive interference therefore dark fringes are formed.

Note:

    • Whenever a wave is reflected from a denser medium, an extra phase difference of π or path difference of λ/2 is introduced.

• Whenever a wave is reflected from a rarer medium, no extra phase difference or path difference is introduced.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Diffraction:

Bending of light rays from sharp edges of an opaque obstacle or aperture and its spreading in the geometrical shadow region is defined as diffraction of light or deviation of light from its rectilinear propagation tendency is defined as diffraction of light.

Conditions of Diffraction:

Path difference at any point on screen due to Fraunhofer diffraction:

$\text { Path difference, } \Delta x=a \sin \theta$

• Size of obstacle or aperture should be nearly equal (Comparable) to the wavelength.

• If size of obstacle/aperture is much larger than wavelength, then diffraction is not observable. (It is practically observed when size of aperture or obstacle is greater than 50λ. The obstacle or aperture does not show diffraction.)

Types of Diffraction

Fresnel diffraction: Both source and screen are near the diffraction device.

Fraunhofer diffraction: Both source and screen are effectively at infinite distances from the diffracting device.

Single slit Diffraction:

$\text {For } n^{\text {th }} \text { secondary minima; } \operatorname{a\sin \theta=n} \lambda \Rightarrow y=\frac{n \lambda D}{a}$

$\text {For } n^{\text {th }} \text { secondary maxima; } a\sin \theta=\frac{(2 n+1) \lambda}{2} \Rightarrow y=\frac{(2 n+1) \lambda D}{2 a}$

$\text{For Central Bright Fringe, Linear width of} \mathrm{CBF}=\frac{2 \lambda \mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{a}}; Angular width of \mathrm{CBF}=2 \sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\mathrm{a}}\right)$

Intensity in Diffraction:

$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{I} & =\mathrm{I}_0\left[\frac{\sin (\beta / 2)}{\beta / 2}\right]^2 \text { and } \beta=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \mathrm{a} \sin \theta \\ I_0 & =\text { intensity of central maxima } \end{aligned}$

Intensity Distribution Curve in Diffraction:
